messages.subject: Trail transect distance analysis
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to analyses a dataset using distance but the method design is a bit untraditional and I would love to receive advice on how to go about it.

A group of connected trails were walked roughly twice per month and an observer recorded detections of various wildlife species (vocal and visual) and estimated the distance and angle of this detection. I have attached a screenshot of the map of the trails to this email. We have about 8 years of such data and we are interested in looking at trends in populations over time. Because the transects follow trails, they are not straight and so we are only able to look at relative abundance, not estimate absolute abundance. Thankfully, the method remain pretty much the same over the 8 year period.

Because there are errors in the dataset with the trail names (change throughtout the years + human error) and trails were sometimes walked more or less than twice during a month, I want to treat each month as 1 single transect with length equal to the length of all the trails walked that month. Thus, its length essentially represents the walking effort for that month. Is it possible to conduct a distance analysis by feeding it data that is presented as 1 transect per month with a different length each month? Remember, we are only interested in changes in relative abundance over time, but we would like to use distance to be able to account for observer effect and detection probability.

Please let me know what you think, how you would go about it, or if you would like any clarifications.

Thank you for your help!
All my best,
Bastien Dehaudt

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Trail transect distance analysis
parts:
Welcome Bastien

Conducting distance sampling surveys along trails creates two problems, neither related to curvature of the trails. First, trails are not placed randomly through the habitat, making extrapolation dubious from the vicinity of the trails to the larger area. Second, animals know where the trails are located; they are either attracted or repelled by the trail violating the assumption that animals area evenly distributed with respect to distance from the trail out to the truncation distance.

By combining transects into a single transect, you lose spatial replication hence cannot estimate variability in encounters between transects. This then negates the ability to make inference from the trails to the wider area. But if it is relative change you wish to measure, perhaps you are content with this price to pay. In which case, you can analyse the data in the manner you describe; mindful of the caveats I mentioned.

Monthly surveys over eight years results in nearly 100 months. You might consider combining data across three or four months to increase sample size for each of the surveys.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Trail transect distance analysis
parts:
Thank you, this is really helpful!

I have another question. If I want to look at changes in relative density between each of the 8 years, does this mean I need to fit a different ds() model for each year of the survey? And then plot the result of the model for each year on a graph (x-axis=year, y-axis=estimated relative density). Or is it possible to run it all in a single model which will give a density estimate for each year? The goal is to look at trends in populations across time. I am using the distance package in R.

Thank you for all your help!

All my best,
Bastien Dehaudt

messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} Re: [distance-sampling] Trail transect distance analysis
parts:
Bastien

You could treat years as "strata" in your analysis. However, the question to answer is whether detectability differs between years.  An example of addressing this question for stratified data is shown here:

https://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-strata/strata-distill.html

You should also note the answer I just gave to Nilanjan regarding his 12 years of data from India. I suggested a third approach for him whereby year could be treated as a covariate in a single detection function model to account for yearly variation in detectability.
